title: Whipped shea and mango body butter
subtitle: A light, fluffy all-over body moisturiser
excerpt: Shea butter and mango butter whipped together with fractionated coconut oil and lavender essential oil. The whipping traps air in the butter and gives it a lighter, faster-absorbing texture. Makes one 150 ml tin.
sourceNotes: Shea butter cosmetic properties: CIR Expert Panel safety assessment of Butyrospermum parkii butter (Cosmetics Ingredient Review, 2015, open access). Mango butter properties: general cosmetic ingredient reference. Fractionated coconut oil as carrier: INCI database reference. Whipping technique for body butters: standard cosmetic formulation practice.

recipe.batchNotes: Doubles easily; use a larger bowl for whipping.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make a batch and store in the tin; keeps six months in a cool place.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Keeps six months in a sealed tin at cool room temperature. Warm weather causes the butter to melt into liquid; refrigerate in summer and whip again when cooled to re-aerate if needed. Discard if the butter smells rancid or develops white spots on the surface.

glossaryTerms.definition: Softened shea or other solid butter beaten with a hand mixer until light and fluffy. The whipping process incorporates air, producing a texture that is easier to spread and absorbs faster than unworked butter.

content.text: body moisturiser for arms, legs, and dry elbows. Shea butter provides long-lasting moisture; mango butter adds a slightly lighter texture; fractionated coconut oil improves spreadability. Whipping the cooled butter with a hand mixer aerates it and makes the finished product feel lighter than a plain balm. The lavender scent is optional but helps with the sensory experience.
Patch test on the inside of the forearm before applying widely. Leave for 24 hours.

content.text: Melt the shea butter and mango butter together in a bowl over a bain-marie until fully liquid. Add the fractionated coconut oil and stir to combine. Pour into a clean mixing bowl and leave to cool to room temperature. For faster cooling, place the bowl in the fridge for 30 to 40 minutes. The butter should be solid but soft: no longer liquid, but it should give easily when pressed. If it is too hard, the whipped texture will be crumbly; if still liquid, return to the fridge.

Beat the cooled butter with a hand mixer on medium speed for about three to four minutes until it is light and fluffy. It will increase in volume by about a third as air is incorporated. Stir in the essential oil by hand if using.
Spoon the whipped butter into the tin and smooth the surface with the back of a spoon. Leave uncovered for one hour to allow any air pockets to settle, then seal the lid.
Scoop a small amount with clean, dry fingers. Apply to dry skin after bathing while the skin is still slightly warm. A little goes a long way.
Keeps six months at cool room temperature. In warm weather the butter may soften to a liquid; refrigerate and re-whip once it firms up again. Discard if the butter smells sharp or rancid.
